key_details: Roof of Unit 3 and turbine hall covered with graphite fragments and fuel particles expelled from Unit 4; highly radioactive (2000-12,000 R/hr in some areas; remote-controlled robots failed due to radiation-induced electronics failure); human 'biorobots' used: 90-second maximum work shift (received ~25 mSv/shift at 1000 R/hr with full PPE); total ~3800-5000 persons participated over August-October 1986; each shift required ~4000 manual operations clearing rubble; debris shoveled into reactor hall hole in Unit 4; roof workers received highest individual doses of any liquidator subgroup; known maximum recorded dose: 1000+ mSv (16,000 mSv estimated for worst positions); 'Order of the Red Banner' awarded to some workers; JEM RADRUE category ROOF: ERR/Gy for leukemia = 1.52 (Ivanov 2004)
source: RADRUE JEM documentation; Pitkevitch 1997 Health Phys; Ivanov 2004 Radiat Environ Biophys; Nyagu 1998; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv; chernobyl_first_responders_medical_REAL.csv

key_details: Tunnel beneath Unit 4: fear that corium would melt through reactor basemat into groundwater (melt-through concern based on incomplete knowledge of corium state); 10,000 miners from Donetsk and Moscow coal basins recruited June 1986; tunnel 168m long; 5.5m wide; completed in 22 days; average tunnel temperature: 50°C; work in 4-hour shifts; primary concern: prevent groundwater contamination and provide cooling for basement floor; tunnel completed but corium did NOT melt through (Elephant's Foot solidified on Level +6; basemat remained intact); nitrogen cooling system installed but never operated (corium cooled naturally); tunnel represents massive mobilization for problem that did not materialize; miners not told actual radiation levels; estimates: individual doses 50-350 mSv for 22-day period
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; Higginbotham 2019 'Midnight in Chernobyl'; corium_fcm_physics_REAL.csv; chernobyl_environmental_remediation_REAL.csv; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv

key_details: Helicopter operations: 5,100 tonnes total material dropped (sand 40%; clay 25%; lead 13%; boron compounds 12%; dolomite 10%); 1,800+ sorties April 27 to May 10; aircraft: Mi-8 and Mi-6 heavy lift; flight path: hover above open reactor → release material → exit; maximum altitude 200m above core initially; reduced to 150m after lead bags failed to drop accurately; pilots: individual doses 10-50 mSv typical; navigators/targeting officers received higher doses; source term second peak May 6-8: helicopter dropping may have temporarily increased releases (disturbing unstable debris); lead: partially melted and vaporized (lead boiling point 1749°C; reactor zone ~1650°C); boron: intended neutron absorption (but reactor already subcritical via melt); sand + clay: reduce volatile release; net effect: limited (materials landed beside or inside but graphite fire continued 14 days)
source: Pazukhin 1994 Radiochimica Acta; source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv; chernobyl_environmental_remediation_REAL.csv; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; Higginbotham 2019

key_details: Decontamination workers: largest subcategory; tasks: washing buildings (fire hoses; polymer film application); scraping/removing topsoil 5-10cm (mechanically and manually); road washing; burial of contaminated materials; felling Red Forest trees (immediately post-accident; chain saws; logging equipment); removing contaminated topsoil from village streets; washing vehicles; most decontamination work: within 30km CEZ; typical dose: 50-500 mSv over full assignment; KID-2 pocket dosimeters provided (0-5 rem range); systematic falsification documented: supervisors assigned workers identical KID-2 readings; group falsification in some units; actual dose underestimate factor 1.5-15×; Prussian Blue not widely distributed to this group; food sometimes from local CEZ (against regulations); RADRUE JEM: dose by location + time + work category + badge record + EPR validation
source: RADRUE JEM documentation 2005; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv; chernobyl_radiation_measurement_instruments_REAL.csv; soviet_civil_defense_response_REAL.csv; retrospective_dosimetry_methods_REAL.csv

key_details: Shelter (sarcophagus) construction: 90,000-100,000 workers over 5 months (July 14 to November 30 1986); constructed reinforced concrete and steel structure 170m×66m×60m entombing Unit 4; work organized in shifts: workers rotated when dose limit reached; original Soviet limit 35 rem = 350 mSv (3.5× IAEA recommendation); raised to 25 rem = 250 mSv during construction; concrete pumped remotely to minimize worker exposure; steel beams placed by cranes; complex mosaic construction from outside-in (workers could not enter core area); specific tasks: concrete pouring 400,000 m³; steel installation 7000 tonnes; lead screen installation; ventilation; deaerator cascade sealed; workers in highest-dose positions (within 50m of reactor) received daily doses of 5-50 mSv; total collective dose: estimated 50,000 person-Sv (Vargo 2000); accelerated aging of sarcophagus structures (concrete cracking under radiation and thermal cycling) = reason NSC needed 30yr later
source: IAEA INSAG-7 1992; Vargo 2000 'The Chernobyl Accident: A Comprehensive Risk Assessment'; chernobyl_shelter_sarcophagus_REAL.csv; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv; unscear_liquidator_doses_REAL.csv

key_details: Firefighters: 134 ARS cases from ~800 first responders; Internal MVD troops and Chernobyl NPP fire brigade; arrived within 7 minutes of explosion; initial response targeted turbine hall roof fires and burning bitumen (believed to be the source of fire); reactor roof: dose rates 1,000-15,000 R/hr; DP-5 field instruments saturated at 200 R/hr showing false '0'; firefighters believed they were responding to ordinary industrial fire; no notification of nuclear accident; PPE: standard fire gear (no dosimetry for most; no respiratory protection for radiation); some firefighters received bone marrow doses estimated 1-16 Gy; classic ARS progression: nausea vomiting diarrhea within 30-120 minutes for highest exposures; transferred to Medchast 126 Pripyat then Hospital No. 6 Moscow; 28 deaths within 3 months (134 ARS cases; all grade 3-4); Pravik dose ~5-6 Gy; Kibenok ~5-6 Gy; Ignatenko ~6-7 Gy; Tischura ~5-6 Gy; Titenok ~5-6 Gy; all from roof access
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; Guskova 2001 J Radiol Prot; ars_cases_REAL.csv; chernobyl_first_responders_medical_REAL.csv; chernobyl_key_persons_REAL.csv; chernobyl_radiation_measurement_instruments_REAL.csv

key_details: Night shift operators April 25-26: ~100 personnel on duty across ChNPP; Unit 4 test team: 24 persons; shift foreman Aleksandr Akimov (dose 15 Gy; died May 11 1986 age 33); reactor control engineer Leonid Toptunov (dose 15+ Gy; died May 16 1986 age 25); after explosion: operators attempted to manage crisis; Akimov and Toptunov tried to provide cooling water (believed reactor intact); worked in high-dose areas multiple hours; operators unaware of true radiation levels (DP-5 showed '0'); control room dose rate: 0.5-3 R/hr (1hr time-weighted average); certain areas of plant: 1000-15,000 R/hr; operators in turbine hall and near-core areas: highest exposures; Dyatlov (deputy chief engineer; supervised test): dose ~5 Gy; survived initially; died 1995 from heart failure; all operators not in immediate core vicinity: 100-500 mSv; RBMK control room: lead shielding partial protection; operators 100m from reactor received ~50× less than reactor hall
source: Plokhy 2018; Higginbotham 2019; chernobyl_key_persons_REAL.csv; ars_cases_REAL.csv; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv; chernobyl_accident_chronology_REAL.csv

key_details: Dosimetric control officers (дозиметристи): responsible for monitoring worker exposure; equipped with: NaI dose rate instruments; direct-reading pocket ionization chambers (KID-2); TLD badges; responsibilities: record worker doses; certify areas safe to work; declare dose limit reached → rotate worker; documented failures: supervisors pressured dosimetrists to record lower values; some dosimetrists falsified records to enable continued work; 'group assignment' = all workers in unit receive same KID-2 value regardless of actual exposure; Pitkevitch 1997 survey: 60% of workers reported incorrect badge readings; Soviet military tradition: 'mission accomplishment > radiation safety'; dosimetrists who refused to falsify faced transfer/discharge; post-Soviet investigation (RADRUE 2005): badge records underestimate by mean factor 2.1 (range 1.5-15); EPR tooth enamel provides most reliable retrospective validation
source: Pitkevitch 1997 Health Phys 72:20-28; RADRUE 2005 Radiat Res 164:551-560; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv; chernobyl_radiation_measurement_instruments_REAL.csv; retrospective_dosimetry_methods_REAL.csv
